content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors introduce NetVec which is a hypergraph embedding system. The main idea is to use a multi-level embedding approach on the star expansion of the hypergraph. Promising experimental results are given for node classification and hyperedge prediction. The authors argue that NetVec is capable to embed very large hypergraphs.
content.main_review:
The proposed system uses a multi-level coarsening strategy reducing the size of the input hypergraph. For this, a hypergraph is represented by a bipartite graph which is an heterogeneous graph structure. The authors assert that NetVec allows to maintain the hypergraph structure through successive levels of coarsening.  The assertion should be proved, i.e. that the coarser graph is a representation of a hypergraph. Indeed, the proposed coarsening algorithm (Algorithm 3 given in appendix) takes as input a simple graph so it is not easy how it works for a bipartite graph representing a hypergraph. It should help the reader to see how the algorithm works over a hypergraph without node features. Also, the output hypergraph is an approximation of the input hypergraph and properties of the transformation should be given.
The second main assertion is the scalability of NetVec. The authors assert that the time complexity of some steps of NetVec are linear in the size of the bipartite representation of the hypergraph. They should give more elements proving their assertions. Also, the time complexity of the complete system NetVec should be studied. 
For the experiments, it should be made precise whether co-authorship or co-citation hypergraphs are used. It is said that the refinement algorithm allows to improve the hypergraph embeddings. Again it is not clear how the algorithm works for bipartite graphs. It should be explained why such an improvement. Last, the choice of the parameter vector w is not discussed.

*** Detailed comments

* Algorithm 1. The input of Coarsening is the bipartite representation of a hypergraph. Consequently, the description of Algorithm 3 should be coherent. The coarsening algorithm should be given in Section 3.1.1, it should take as input a bipartite graph representing a hypergraph, it should clearly output a bipartite graph representing a hypergraph. What is f? How do you compute the embedding of a bipartite graph with a graph embedding designed for simple graphs? What is $\tilde{u}$?
* Section 3.1.1 It is not easy to understand the algorithm without a clear distinction between the two types of nodes. The assertion at the end of the section ("One important point ....") should be proved. Also it is said that "a coarser graph represents the original hypergraph". In my opinion, the coarser graph is an approximation of the original hypergraph and properties of such an approximation should be studied.
* Section 3.1.2. As said before, you should comment how you compute the embedding of the coarsest hypergraph using a system designed for simple graphs.
* Section 3.1.3. It is said that the vector w is made of weights and then that the algorithm can be improved using a hyper-parameter vector w. This is not discussed further in the paper. Thus it is not clear how to choose such an hyper-parameter and it is not said how t it is chosen in the experiments.
* Section 3. A subsection should be devoted to the study of the time complexity of NetVec.
* Section 4. Dataset description. Please precise which hypergraph is considered (co-authorship or co-citation). Please make precise what is the number of edges. Is it the number of edges in the star representation?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper introduces a new system for computing unsupervised hypergraph embeddings. The considered problem is significant and difficult. The main idea is to use a multi-level embedding approach on the star expansion of the hypergraph. This seems promising but, in my opinion, the descriptions of the algorithms are rather vague and do not allow to be fully convinced by the main assertions of the paper. Also, a more complete study of the time complexity should be provided in the paper. Therefore, despite promising ideas and promising experimental results, I think that the paper is not ready for publication at ICLR.

content.title: Additional Clarifications
content.comment:
**coarsening algorithm (Algorithm 3 given in appendix) takes as input a simple graph**
- The input to the coarsening is the star expansion of the hypergraph. 

**It should be made precise whether co-authorship or co-citation hypergraphs are used**
Cora, Citeseer, and PubMed are cocitation, DBLP is co-authorship. We will clarify this in the submission.

**Is it the number of edges in the star representation?**
- Yes

**It is not clear how the algorithm works for bipartite graphs**
- The inputs to all three levels of the framework is a bipartite graph. The key difference between processing graphs and processing the bipartite representation of a hypergraph is that the processing of nodes in the bipartite graph is type-dependent: we process the nodes representing hyperedges differently from how we process nodes representing the hypergraph nodes.

**It should be explained why such an improvement.**
- The improvement is because the refinement algorithm, which performs Laplacian smoothing, eliminates high-frequency noise. Intuitively, we expect graphs to have the “homophily” property, which means that nodes that close together in the hypergraph are expected to have similar labels. Laplacian smoothing eliminates “spikes” in the embeddings of adjacent nodes and brings their embeddings closer together, exploiting homophily. This is explained in section 3.1.3.

**Choice of the parameter vector w is not discussed**
- We use 0.5. This makes the importance of neighboring nodes as well as the embedding of a node in the previous level the same. 

**You should comment how you compute the embedding of the coarsest hypergraph using a system designed for simple graphs.**
- We use an edgelist of the coarsest bipartite graph as an input to a graph embedding algorithm such as node2vec.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a heuristic multi-level approach for computing node embeddings of hypergraphs.
content.main_review:
**Strengths:**

Hypergraphs are a generalization of graphs and they arise in many application domains. This paper proposes a multi-level approach that scalably computes hypergraph node embeddings.

**Major weaknesses:**

Unfortunately there are two major issues with this paper. First, the proposed method contains too many, if not all, heuristic constructions that, in my opinion, may not make sense in general. Second, the empirical evaluations are missing important information about the datasets and details of the experiments, and hence, the reported results may be potentially misleading. 

In what follows I provide details.

*About the proposed methods:*

1. Why is mean aggregation (instead of other possible aggregation methods) used to compute the feature vector of a hyperedge? Some discussions are needed to justify the choice.

2. When assigning nodes to hyperedges, why is the cosine similarity used? Can we use other similarity measures? My guess is that the authors use the cosine similarity because in their experiments for node classification, the datasets are citation networks and the node feature vectors come from bag-of-words encoding. In these datasets, cosine similarity aligns well with class labels. However, no explanation is ever provided for the choice of cosine similarity in general. Discussions on the choice of similarity measure in the coarsening step should be provided.

3. When assigning nodes to hyperedges, and when the hypergraph does not have node features, the authors suggest to compute some "importance" measure, e.g., w_j/d_j. But what if w_j = d_j for all j? The authors suggest to break the tie randomly, but in this extreme case when we randomly assign every node to an arbitrary hyperedge in the coarsening step, will the method still provide meaningful embeddings? More explanations and discussions are needed.

4. How many iterations of refinement (i.e., Laplacian smoothing) is suggested? Table 5 in the appendix (not in Section 4) seems to empirically demonstrate that around 30 iterations is sufficient for the citation networks, but why 30, not 5? Moreover, why does the improvement stops after around 100 iterations? Is it due to the fact that Laplacian smoothing converges reasonably after 100 iterations, or due to the fact that for these citation networks, local network structure (i.e., locally smoothed feature vectors) is already very informative about the class labels, so global network structure (i.e., fully smoothed feature vectors) is not useful? Some discussions should be provided either in the main text or in the appendix.

*About the experiments*

1. The paper does not provide a citation for the datasets in Table 1. The authors claim that they "[use] the standard hypergraph datasets from prior works", but I could not find verify the source of the datasets. For example, the Cora dataset that the authors provided in the supplementary material does not match with the Cora dataset used in [Yadati et al. (2019)] or the one used in [1]. The original Cora dataset has 2708 nodes, why is the Cora dataset used in this paper has only 1434 nodes? I tried to keep the largest connected component, but I still get slightly less than 2400 nodes.

2. Since the source of datasets is not clear to me, I cannot verify the validity of the empirical results. I suggest the authors use the same publicly available datasets used by [Yadati et al. (2019)], and follow the same train/test splits. This will ensure consistency for comparing methods and results reported across papers. Moreover, it will improve reproducibility. Please also include other datasets in the supplementary material, e.g., Citeseer, Pubmed, DBLP, right now the supplementary material only contains the Cora datasets. 

3. The authors should compare their method with [1] and [2]. [2] is particularly relevant because [2] is also an *unsupervised* node embedding method for hypergraphs. Maybe more importantly, Table 2 in [2] shows that the method in [2] is significantly better than the method proposed in this paper, for all the node classification tasks. But, as I mentioned in my previous point, the empirical settings may be very different. This highlights the importance of using the same benchmark hypergraphs and the same train/test splits. For example, for the Cora dataset, please report a test result when using 20 labelled nodes from each of the 7 classes. [1] applies GCN to the clique expansion of hypergraphs, so [1] is relevant and the authors should compare with [1].

4. Once node embeddings are obtained, how did you perform node classification? Did you train a multi-class classification model? If so, what 
loss function did you use?

**Minor**

1. In high-order network analysis, people usually refer the number of nodes connected by a hyperedge as the order of that hyperedge. It might be helpful to add this as a footnote, as the term "degree" of a hyperedge sounds a bit less common.

2. The authors claim generality as a contribution in this work. However, without specific experiments on graphs (not hypergraphs), I could not see how generality is particularly important.

3. In Section 2.1, it might be more clear if graph embedding methods are categorized into supervised and unsupervised approaches.

4. Please discuss the details about parallel implementation in the appendix.

**Additional references**

[1] Hypergraph Neural Networks. Yifan Feng, Haoxuan You, Zizhao Zhang, Rongrong Ji, Yue Gao. 2019 \
[2] A nonlinear diffusion method for semi-supervised learning on hypergraphs. Francesco Tudisco, Konstantin Prokopchik, Austin R. Benson. 2021.
content.summary_of_the_review: The multi-level hypergraph embedding method proposed in this paper, while mildly interesting, is neither novel nor surprising. Moreover, the method contains too many heuristics without proper justifications. As an empirical paper, the empirical evaluations are rather weak: A number of important details are missing, making it hard to verify the validity of the results.

content.title: Additional Clarifications
content.comment:
**Why is mean aggregation (instead of other possible aggregation methods) used to compute the feature vector of a hyperedge? Some discussions are needed to justify the choice.**
- We could use other methods such as geometric means. However, mean aggregation is fast and also produces a good approximation of a feature vector for hyperedges because it minimizes the two-norm of the sum of the distances between the hyperedge embedding and the node embeddings.

**When assigning nodes to hyperedges, why is the cosine similarity used?**
- We tried other binary operators such as L1 and L2 distance. However, cosine similarity was working just as well as these alternatives. 

**The authors suggest to break the tie randomly, but in this extreme case when we randomly assign every node to an arbitrary hyperedge in the coarsening step, will the method still provide meaningful embeddings?**
- In such cases the nodes will be randomly assigned to a hyperedge that is connected to so the structural similarity would be exploited and the method would be meaningful.

**How many iterations of refinement (i.e., Laplacian smoothing) is suggested?**
- We show experimentally that 30 iterations of refinement is good enough for the datasets in our study. This is similar to the GCN approaches when they are selecting the number of layers for GCNs. Performing a lot more iterations of refinement may result in what is called  “Laplacian over-smoothing” and may reduce the accuracy of the inference tasks. 

**The paper does not provide a citation for the datasets in Table 1**
- All the inputs used for node classification in this paper are the same as those used in HyperGCN: https://github.com/malllabiisc/HyperGCN/tree/master/data. We performed some preprocessing as explained below.


**I could not verify the source of the datasets. For example, the Cora dataset that the authors provided in the supplementary material does not match with the Cora dataset used in [Yadati et al. (2019)]**
- The dataset is the same. We do some preprocessing as mentioned in the paper: nodes not connected to any hyperedge, as well as hyperedges containing only one hypernode, were removed. Perhaps you are counting the number of hyperedges as well as nodes for cora since if you count all the nodes that participate in at least a hyperedge, for cora, it will add up to 1,434. We double checked to verify this. If you cannot get these results, we would appreciate it if you share with us how you are counting the nodes so we can figure out where the discrepancy is.

**I suggest the authors use the same publicly available datasets used by [Yadati et al. (2019)], and follow the same train/test splits.** 
- HyperGCN only provides10 different train/test splits which is not enough for taking an average and reporting the standard deviation. In order to show improvements are statistically significant, we have to show the averaged over several different random weight initializations and train/test splits. 

**The authors should compare their method with [1] and [2]. [2] is particularly relevant because [2] is also an unsupervised node embedding method for hypergraphs.**
- Unfortunately, the code for [2] is not available to compare with. Also [2] is a semi-supervised approach for node embedding method for hypergraphs, whereas ours is unsupervised. We did not compare with [1] since HyperGCN reported superior results compared to [1]. 

**Once node embeddings are obtained, how did you perform node classification? Did you train a multi-class classification model? If so, what loss function did you use?**
- Yes, we applied logistic regression and used cross-entropy loss.

content.title: Further comments
content.comment:
Thank you for your clarifications. Even though I still have major concerns as I will explain below, I appreciate your time for answering my questions in detail.

> The dataset is the same. We do some preprocessing as mentioned in the paper: nodes not connected to any hyperedge, as well as hyperedges containing only one hypernode, were removed. Perhaps you are counting the number of hyperedges as well as nodes for cora since if you count all the nodes that participate in at least a hyperedge, for cora, it will add up to 1,434. We double checked to verify this. If you cannot get these results, we would appreciate it if you share with us how you are counting the nodes so we can figure out where the discrepancy is.

During my initial review I used the coauthorship dataset. I noticed from your response to Reviewer vdRS that you used Cora cocitation dataset. You are right, the cocitation network has 1,434 nodes after removing all singletons. But it has 1,079 edges, not 2,708 edges. Is this a typo in your current Table 1?

> Unfortunately, the code for [2] is not available to compare with. Also [2] is a semi-supervised approach for node embedding method for hypergraphs, whereas ours is unsupervised.

The method in [2] that computes node embeddings is unsupervised. In fact, the way that [2] performs node classification is exactly the same as yours. [2] applies logistic regression for node classification, after obtaining the node embeddings in a fully unsupervised approach. The algorithm in [2] is very simple and thus should be fairly straightforward to implement, e.g., in 1-2 hours. Moreover, the results reported in [2] are significantly better than the results you obtained in Table 2, e.g., [2] had 82.8% for Cora, 72% for Citeseer, and 89.1% for DBLP, whereas you had 67.7% for Cora, 60.6% for Citeseer, and 78.5% for DBLP.

>  We did not compare with [1] since HyperGCN reported superior results compared to [1].

In my experience, properly tuned HGNN [1] can have much better performance than the ones in Table 2. For example, with 4% labels HGNN can get ~89% accuracy for DBLP (note that this is ~10% higher than the best one in your Table 2). On the other hand, I believe that HyperGCN should have better performance than the ones reported in your Table 2 as well, if properly tuned. I suggest the authors spend additional efforts tuning the baselines.

> We show experimentally that 30 iterations of refinement is good enough for the datasets in our study. This is similar to the GCN approaches when they are selecting the number of layers for GCNs. Performing a lot more iterations of refinement may result in what is called "Laplacian over-smoothing" and may reduce the accuracy of the inference tasks.

(This is minor.) For GCNs I don't think the concept of "over-smoothing" referred by some practitioners is widely accepted. Even though there are some rigorous investigations into this, e.g., Oono and Suzuki, ICLR 2020, in order to guarantee "over-smoothing", one usually require many assumptions and the number of layers go to infinity. In practice, a performance degradation for deeper GCNs might just be due to over-fitting.

content.title: Further comments
content.comment:
**Is this a typo in your current Table 1?**
- Yes, we will fix this. Thank you.
**The algorithm in [2] is very simple and thus should be fairly straightforward to implement, e.g., in 1-2 hours. Moreover, the results reported in [2] are significantly better than the results you obtained in Table 2, e.g., [2] had 82.8% for Cora, 72% for Citeseer, and 89.1% for DBLP, whereas you had 67.7% for Cora, 60.6% for Citeseer, and 78.5% for DBLP.**
- We will include these results in the future revisions of the paper. However, we believe these two papers address slightly different problems. Our paper not only focuses on embedding quality but also scalability for embedding on large hypergraphs. While [2] mentions their approach scales linearly with the number and size of the hyperedges, they use clique expansions to convert hypergraphs to graphs.  The use of this representation is fundamentally less scalable than the star expansion we build on in NetVec.  As a concrete example, for the Friendster dataset, the star expansion produces a graph with 37,783,346 edges while the clique expansion would have 460,844,112 edges. Accordingly, we believe that algorithms that build on the star-expansion are fundamentally the correct way to create practical and scalable systems for processing large hypergraphs.  

- Another major difference is that [2] only focuses on node classification for hypergraphs and it is not clear how one would apply the same method for hyperedge prediction.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper provides a multi-level approach to learning embeddings for hypergraphs which can be used for downstream tasks of node classification and hyperedge prediction. The proposed method, NetVec, is based on the principle of coarsening a hypergraph followed by employing existing techniques (in this case, node2vec) of learning embeddings and refining the embeddings for the original hypergraph. Authors have shown that the coarsening and refinement procedure let them get embeddings for hypergraphs with more than a million nodes in a few seconds. The proposed method is tested on multiple datasets for node classification and hyperedge prediction and improves performance over the baselines considered.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
a) The paper takes one of the most important problems in the space of hypergraphs. Most of the solutions that work for hypergraphs do not scale well because of the intrinsic complexity of hypergraph structure.
b) The proposed framework of obtaining node embeddings works well for all the datasets in the case of node classification and most of the cases in hyperedge prediction. The paper tests NetVec on a variety of datasets, and the numbers outperform the baselines used.

Weaknesses:
a) I am concerned about the novelty of the proposed framework. Working with a coarsened hypergraph and refining the solution for the original hypergraph is not new. There is a separate line of work focused on this aspect of hypergraphs, mainly in the context of clustering [1]. It is possible that the existing coarsening methods may not suit well in your settings, but the paper never talks about them.
b) Choice of baselines: The baselines used, especially in the case of hyperedge prediction, are not sufficient. Node2Vec is a graph-based method, so comparing against it doesn't reveal much. There are other recent methods of hyperedge prediction that this paper does not discuss [2, 3]. Comparing the accuracy of the proposed method that uses both higher-order information and node features against a technique that uses neither is a weak comparison.

Suggestions for improvement:
a) The rationale behind choosing node2vec to obtain an initial set of embeddings is not clear. More advanced methods (GCN and its later versions) use attribute information to get embeddings for graphs, which node2vec does not consider.
b) Since the paper proposes a coarsening/refinement framework and not any embedding/classification/hyperedge prediction method, an additional but more fundamental way of evaluation could be the visualization of embeddings.

Clarifications:
a) How did you apply graph-based baselines on hypergraphs? Do you take clique reduction? Star expansion? or some other reduction?
b) In Table 2, how come node2vec takes more time than NetVec(l=2)? My understanding is that NetVec(l=2) runs a node2vec in addition to coarsening and refinement steps. Can you please add some explanation on what I am missing here?
c) In the Introduction, don't say, "Two hypergraph problems have been studied in the literature: node classification and hyperedge prediction." There are a lot more hypergraph-based research problems in the literature.
d) The "importance" defined in section 3.1.1 will assign low importance to the nodes that are part of large hyperedges. Can you explain the rationale behind this choice in the context of your datasets?

Questions during rebuttal period: Kindly respond to the questions asked in clarifications and your take on the points raised in weaknesses and suggestions for improvement.

1. Papa, David A., and Igor L. Markov. "Hypergraph Partitioning and Clustering." Handbook of Approximation Algorithms and Metaheuristics 20073547 (2007): 61-1.
2. Yadati, Naganand, et al. "NHP: Neural hypergraph link prediction." Proceedings of the 29th ACM International Conference on Information & Knowledge Management. 2020.
3. Kumar, Tarun, et al. "HPRA: Hyperedge prediction using resource allocation." 12th ACM Conference on Web Science. 2020.

content.title: Additional Clarifications
content.comment:
**Working with a coarsened hypergraph and refining the solution for the original hypergraph is not new. There is a separate line of work focused on this aspect of hypergraphs, mainly in the context of clustering**
- The paper you referred to uses coarsening in the context of hypergraph partitioning. We have mentioned this in our paper. Using a multi-level approach for hypergraph embedding has not been explored previously. Finally, no previous work on hypergraph partitioning has been able to utilise node features in their coarsening method.
**There are other recent methods of hyperedge prediction that this paper does not discuss [2, 3]**
- Thank you for pointing that out. We will include the results for these approaches.

**Comparing the accuracy of the proposed method that uses both higher-order information and node features against a technique that uses neither is a weak comparison.**
- We believe not being able to use node features is a weakness of a method. For example, MILE has no technique to use node features. In our framework, we are proposing a way to do so. Approaches such as MILE can adopt this idea and utilise node features for better node embedding quality

**The rationale behind choosing node2vec to obtain an initial set of embeddings is not clear.**
- The initial embedding is not a contribution of our approach. Any network embedding approach can be used and we picked node2vec only because the multi-level frameworks that we used as our baselines are all compatible with node2vec.
We can add results for computing the initial embedding for other approaches such as DeepWalk and GCNs.

**an additional but more fundamental way of evaluation could be the visualization of embeddings**
- Thanks for the suggestion. We will add that. 
**How did you apply graph-based baselines on hypergraphs?**
- We used the star expansion for all methods. We also tried clique expansion for graph based methods and it didn’t change the quality of results but it made the approaches slower. 
**how come node2vec takes more time than NetVec(l=2).**
- If the graph is big enough, the slowest part of the multi-level embedding approach is the initial embedding. Coarsening reduces the size of the hypergraph so initial embedding and refinement can be done faster. So if the graph is big enough, two levels of coarsening should reduce the runtime compared to 0 level. You can see the effect of coarsening in running time in larger graphs such as DBLP, and Friendster, MovieLens, DRUG, and WordNet. 

**The "importance" defined in section 3.1.1 will assign low importance to the nodes that are part of large hyperedges.**
- If each node in a hyperedge contributes 1/m to that hyperedge where m is the degree of the hyperedge, the contribution of a node in a low degree hyperedge is larger than a larger degree hyperedge.

content.title: Thank you for the response.
content.comment:
Thank you for providing the clarifications. You have answered many of my concerns. My response is given below.

1. Separate line of work: Yes, you did mention the related coarsening work, but you don't set the contrast between the two approaches. I don't want you to compare against those approaches, but a few comments on the differences, and how your approach may work better in the cases where they don't, would be helpful to give the complete picture.
2. Recent methods: Seeing those numbers (or at least a method-level comparison) would be helpful while revising the overall score.
3. Regarding baselines: This is related to point (2). You can use Hypergraph-based link prediction methods. Similarly, in node classification using GCN, HyperGCN (which you did) and their recent versions make more sense than using node2vec.
4. The rationale behind choosing node2vec: Yes, I understand that the proposed framework is not dependent on the initial embedding. My point is, when you have feature-level information why not use it? If you use feature level information (by using GCN or some other method) and then analyse the performance gain, that will show the actual strength of your work.
5. Visualization: Ok.
6. Graph-based baselines: This was not clear from the text, please add it in the experiments section. Typically, people use clique-based expansions and then use graph-based baselines. You can mention your reasoning in the paper.
7. node2vec takes more time: Got it. Thanks for the clarification.
8. The "importance"score: I understood the formula but I couldn't get the rationale behind it. For instance, if you want to define a diffusion operator on a hypergraph, where the information is diffused over hyperedges and then to nodes, assigning low importance to the nodes which are part of large hyperedges makes sense. I am trying to understand your reasoning of choosing such a mechanism.

replying_to: Replying to Thank you for the response.

content.title: Thank you for your comments
content.comment:
**1-7**
- Thank you for your suggestions. They makes sense and we will add those in the future revisions.
**8**
- Our reasoning is very similar to what you mentioned.   A node in a small hyperedge is more local to that hyperedge compared to a large hyperedge. In context of social network this mechanism makes more sense. For example, in a community network such as facebook, where hyperedges are communities and nodes are users, the "democratic party"community  gives you less information than "MIT class of 2021" community.
Experimentally, we tried various approaches such as random, low/high degree, low/high weight, etc. and this mechanism worked the best in most cases.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper focuses on the problem of representing nodes in hyperedges in a low-dimensional Euclidean space. The approach is a heuristic algorithm that hierarchically reduces the problem to simple graph embedding (here and henceforth I use "simple graph" as a technical term).
content.main_review:
My main concern for the publication is novelty and unfair experimental comparisons. The proposed algorithm is a simple heuristic that does not look any better than previous work – GraphZoom has some theoretical insights from theory of spectral sparsification while MILE has some social science theory-inspired heuristics. The contraction operation seems extremely similar to HARP [Chen et al., 2017] as an extension to hypergraphs.

There is not much to discuss about the technical quality and exposition of the paper, since the contribution is a heuristic naïve baseline. The performance is aggravating for a method that uses node features – 70% for Cora means very poor embedding quality (simple GCN achieves 80%+, modern 83-85%). I am particularly skeptical, since GraphZoom reports 83+% accuracy on that standard dataset. Overall, it it confusing that some baselines use the node features, while some do not. I would suggest to add some indication of that into the results tables.

One other experimental problem I have noticed is the lengths of random walks used in node2vec. Instead of the standard 80, allowing to explore the graph more, here it's merely 20. I can imagine this severely cripples that baseline.

Overall, this is a paper without any theoretical contributions, so I believe it should be evaluated on its empirical effectiveness. The effectiveness was not sufficiently demonstrated in the paper, and I have serious doubts about the efficacy of the proposed approach, as it fails to perform on too-simple-to-fail datasets, such as Cora.
content.summary_of_the_review: The overall contributions of the paper are marginal – there is no theoretical insight to the proposed folding technique, and the experiments are mostly comparing against simple graph embedding baselines.

content.title: Additional Clarifications
content.comment:
**The contraction operation seems extremely similar to HARP**
- Our approach has major differences from HARP. HARP handles only graphs and the extension from  graphs to hypergraphs is non trivial. There are many ways to coarsen a hypergraph and the method described in the submission performs the best in terms of both quality and running time. In addition, our coarsening algorithm utilises node features while HARP cannot utilise node features. 
**The performance is aggravating for a method that uses node features – 70% for Cora means very poor embedding quality (simple GCN achieves 80%+, modern 83-85%)**
- The Cora dataset is a directed citation graph and we agree that using a GCN achieves an accuracy of 80+%. What we show in the paper is that if you look at this dataset as a co-citation hypergraph as in [1] our approach is superior to all the baselines.
[1] Naganand Yadati, Madhav Nimishakavi, Prateek Yadav, Vikram Nitin, Anand Louis, and Partha Talukdar. Hypergcn: A new method of training graph convolutional networks on hypergraphs, 2019
**I have noticed is the lengths of random walks used in node2vec. Instead of the standard 80, allowing to explore the graph more, here it's merely 20. I can imagine this severely cripples that baseline.** 
- The settings used for node2vec are the best we could find. For example, if we use 80 for the length of the random walk, the accuracy drops to 46.7% for DBLP while the current setting results in 67.1% for node2vec. 

**this is a paper without any theoretical contributions, so I believe it should be evaluated on its empirical effectiveness. The effectiveness was not sufficiently demonstrated in the paper**
- We have shown the performance of our approach on small and large datasets on different tasks(node classification and link prediction) while previous approaches only worked on one but not both. We have also done an ablation study on different parts of this framework. We would appreciate it if the referee explains what additional evaluation we should do. 

**it fails to perform on too-simple-to-fail datasets, such as Cora**
- Please see above.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The main goal of the paper is to introduce a scalable algorithm for generating hypergraph embeddings to be subsequently used for node classification and hyperedge predictions tasks.
content.main_review:
The problem is important and timely, and has attracted significant interest in recent years due to its applicability. Existing sota methods still lack in performance.  

The present work puts forth a nice idea of jointly embedding the edges and the hyperedges, and departs from the traditional approaches for hypergraphs that do a clique or star expansions.

The experimental results are fairly convincing and appear to be fair, though additional data sets could have been employed, with various levels of size and sparsity. The proposed methods clearly outperforms competition in terms of running time, and most often also in terms of accuracy.

Would have been good to assess performance on a stochastic block model for hypergraphs, to see how close to the ground truth one gets in such synthetic models.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The experimental section could be further strengthened.

Later edit:
It appears that the authors did not compare to other task-relevant sota methods, as other reviewers have pointed out.
